For example: the 25 prophets mentioned by name, the categories of people (mu'minoon, kafireen etc.), the prohibited things (haram), the signs of Qiyamah, the names/attributes of Allah (Asma ul Husna), angels mentioned by name, animals mentioned, stories/parables, punishments (hudood), pillars of Islam mentioned, rivers of paradise, levels of hell (Jahannam), days/events of the afterlife sequence, battles mentioned, etc. I want a comprehensive meta-list of every topic in the Quran that has a finite enumerable set of items that a researcher would want to list completely.

For example: the 25 prophets mentioned by name, the categories of people (mu'minoon, kafireen etc.), the prohibited things (haram), the signs of Qiyamah, the names/attributes of Allah (Asma ul Husna), angels mentioned by name, animals mentioned, stories/parables, punishments (hudood), pillars of Islam mentioned, rivers of paradise, levels of hell (Jahannam), days/events of the afterlife sequence, battles mentioned, etc. I want a comprehensive meta-list of every topic in the Quran that has a finite enumerable set of items that a researcher would want to list completely.
result.summary: The Quran contains numerous enumerable lists that scholars and researchers have catalogued across centuries of Islamic scholarship. The most robustly verified sets include: categories of people and religious communities (nine distinct groups), specific dietary prohibitions (eleven items across multiple verses), the Five Pillars of Islam (five items, from hadith tradition), and a small set of named parables (five, per Wikipedia's enumeration). Other commonly cited enumerations — such as the 25 named prophets, the seven levels of Jahannam, the named angels, the signs of Qiyamah, and animals mentioned — were not verified to a sufficient evidentiary standard in this research pass and should be treated as provisional. A key finding is that some items traditionally attributed to the Quran (such as the punishment of stoning/rajm) exist in hadith tradition but not in the compiled Mushaf, illustrating the boundary between Quranic and post-Quranic enumeration.

findings.claim: The Quran identifies nine distinct, enumerable categories of people and religious communities: People of the Book, Jews, Christians, Sabians, Magians, Muslims, Hypocrites, Disbelievers, and Polytheists.
findings.evidence: All nine categories have explicit Arabic Quranic terms used repeatedly across the text. Ahl al-Kitab, Yahud, Nasara, As-Sabi'un, Majus, Muslimoon/Mu'minoon, Munafiqoon, Kafireen, and Mushrikeen are each named in multiple surahs. Note that 'People of the Book' partially overlaps with Jews, Christians, and sometimes Sabians, so these are not mutually exclusive categories.

findings.claim: The Quran enumerates a specific finite set of dietary prohibitions across multiple verses: carrion/dead animals, flowing blood, pork, animals slaughtered in the name of other than Allah, strangulated animals, animals killed by a blow, those that fell to their death, those gored by horns, those eaten by predators, animals sacrificed on stone altars, and intoxicants.
findings.evidence: Quran 2:173 lists four core prohibitions; 5:3 extends the list with six additional categories of improperly slaughtered animals; 5:90 prohibits intoxicants. A scholarly nuance exists: 6:145 presents only four prohibitions, and some interpreters argue this is the complete list, making 5:3 additions context-specific rather than universal additions. The mainstream position across Sunni schools of jurisprudence accepts all listed items. This makes the set enumerable but not without some scholarly boundary dispute.

findings.claim: The Five Pillars of Islam as enumerated in Sunni tradition constitute exactly five items: Shahada, Salah, Zakat, Sawm, and Hajj.
findings.evidence: The Five Pillars as a set of exactly five is established in primary hadith sources (Sahih Bukhari 8, Sahih Muslim 16), which enumerate them precisely. The set is stable across centuries of Sunni scholarship. Importantly, the Five Pillars as a named set are a hadith-derived framework — individual pillars are mentioned in the Quran but the Quran does not enumerate them as 'five pillars' in a single passage. The Shia tradition has a different framework (ten Furoo al-Din), confirming this enumeration is tradition-specific.

findings.claim: Wikipedia's article on Quranic parables identifies five named parables with Quranic references: The Hamlet in Ruins (2:259), The Two Gardens (18:32-44), The Worldly Life (18:45-46), Those who associate partners with God (22:73-74), and The House of the Spider (29:41).
findings.evidence: The Wikipedia article was directly verified to contain exactly these five named parables with the matching references. However, this list likely reflects only formally named/titled parables in Western academic literature, not the full scope of Quranic analogies and similitudes (amthal), which classical Islamic scholars enumerate as far more numerous. This should be treated as a partial enumeration for researchers rather than a complete canonical list.

findings.claim: A body of Quranic topic indices confirms that behavioral, legal, and doctrinal categories — including adultery, alcohol, apostasy, and alliances — are treated as discrete enumerable regulated or prohibited topics in Quranic literature.
findings.evidence: Direct verification of the searchtruth.com topic index confirms these appear as distinct indexed categories. This confirms the methodological point that Quranic prohibitions and regulations form enumerable topical clusters, even if the exact count of prohibited items varies by interpretive school. The source is a secondary topic index rather than a primary scholarly enumeration.

findings.claim: The hadith tradition records that stoning (rajm) for married adulterers was considered a revealed Quranic verse by Umar ibn al-Khattab, though it does not appear in the compiled Mushaf — illustrating the boundary between Quranic enumeration and hadith-derived legal content.
sources: Sahih Bukhari 6830 (Agreed Upon / also in Sahih Muslim)
findings.evidence: Sahih al-Bukhari 6830 directly records Umar ibn al-Khattab stating that the verse of rajm was revealed but expressing fear it would be denied because it is not in the written Mushaf. This is the highest tier of Sunni hadith authenticity (Mutawatir/'Agreed Upon'). This finding is methodologically important for any researcher building enumerable Quranic lists: several items traditionally associated with Quranic law derive from hadith, not the Mushaf text itself, and the two must be distinguished.

result.caveats: Several high-profile enumerations that are commonly cited in Islamic scholarship were not verified to sufficient evidentiary standard in this research pass and should be treated as unconfirmed pending further primary-source verification: (1) The canonical 25 named prophets — the list is widely cited but the specific count and membership was refuted in adversarial verification, suggesting the number and membership varies by scholarly tradition. (2) Named angels in the Quran — the corpus.quran.com source for this claim was refuted (0-3 votes). (3) The seven levels/gates of Jahannam and their names — refuted (0-3) despite being a commonly repeated claim; the Quran mentions seven gates in 15:44 but does not name the levels. (4) Signs of Qiyamah — no canonical fixed list was verified; the set is drawn from hadith collections, not solely the Quran, and varies across scholarly traditions. (5) Animals mentioned in the Quran — multiple attempts to verify a specific count (12, 13, or other numbers) all failed adversarial review. Researchers should note that many 'Quranic enumerations' in popular Islamic literature blend Quranic text with hadith material, tafsir traditions, and scholarly inference, which complicates clean enumeration. The Five Pillars in particular are a hadith-derived framework, not a Quranic list. Sources used were predominantly secondary (Wikipedia, topic index websites); primary Quranic text verification was done for dietary prohibitions only.

refuted.claim: The Quranic Arabic Corpus topic index lists four angels mentioned by name in the Quran: Jibreel, Mikaeel, Malik, and Azrael.
The topic index identifies approximately twelve animals mentioned in the Quran, including camel, cow, horse, dog, bird, fish, ant, bee, spider, locust, frog, and ape.

The topic index organizes Quranic content into broad enumerable categories including prophets, angels, animals, places, religious concepts, natural elements, foods and plants, materials and objects, body parts, and historical events.

The hadith specifies three distinct evidentiary conditions that trigger the hudood punishment of rajm: witnessed evidence, pregnancy (conception), or personal confession — making the set of triggering conditions finite and enumerable.
The Quran mentions exactly 13 distinct animals by name, forming a finite enumerable set: ape, camel, cow, dog, frog, goat, horse, lion, mule, pig, sheep, snake, and wolf.

The Quran mentions exactly 25 prophets and messengers by name, including Adam, Idris, Nuh, Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Lut, Ismail, Ishaq, Yaqub, Yusuf, Ayyub, Shuayb, Musa, Harun, Dawud, Sulayman, Ilyas, al-Yasaa, Yunus, Zakariyya, Yahya, Isa, and Muhammad.

The site enumerates specific animals mentioned in the Quran including ants, apes, beasts, bees, birds, cattle, dogs, donkeys, elephants, and horses — providing a finite enumerable list of Quranic animals.
The site lists specific communities and peoples addressed in the Quran as a finite set: Ad, Bedouins, Christians, Jews, Thamud, and Pharaoh's people.

The site partially lists prophets mentioned by name in the Quran including Abraham, Aaron, Adam, David, Elijah, Elisha, Idris, Isaac, Ishmael, Jacob, Jesus, and Joseph — but the extracted list appears incomplete relative to the canonical 25 named prophets.

The site presents Believers (mu'minoon) as a standalone enumerable category, implying categories of people in the Quran (believers, disbelievers, bedouin, Jews and Christians, etc.) are tracked as discrete enumerable groups.

There is no single canonical accepted list of signs of the end times agreed upon by Sunni or Shia Muslims, making any enumeration of Qiyamah signs a matter of scholarly variation rather than a fixed finite set.

The major signs include specific named figures and events: the Dajjal, the Mahdi, the return of Isa (Jesus), the Sufyani, and Yajuj and Majuj (Gog and Magog), as well as large-scale battles and natural disasters.

The Quran presents the afterlife as a structured sequence of five stages: death, the intermediate world (Barzakh), Resurrection (Qiyamah), Judgment (Hisab), and the ultimate destinations of Paradise (Jannah) and Hell (Jahannam).
Jahannam has seven gates and seven levels, with the Quran explicitly stating 'seven gates and for every gate there shall be a specific party of sinners' (Q.15:43-44)
The seven named levels of Jahannam are: Jahannam, al-Laza, al-Hutama, al-Sa'ir, al-Saqar, al-Jahim, and al-Hawiya
Al-Kaffarah comprises exactly 5 primary categories: unintentional/semi-unintentional murder, fasting violations, breaking oaths, Hajj (ihram violations), and zihar (a pre-Islamic divorce method).

The kaffarah for breaking an oath consists of three alternative expiations: feeding 10 poor people, clothing them, or releasing a slave — with fasting 3 days as a fallback — as derived from Quran 66:2.
The Quran explicitly enumerates 13 items that are haram (forbidden to eat), forming a finite, textually grounded list of dietary prohibitions.
There are exactly 10 major signs (alamat al-sa'ah al-kubra) of the Day of Judgement listed in Islamic eschatology, ending with the blowing of the Trumpet.
